title: Sebastian and the Visitor
premise: Orsen Kavanagh, a property surveyor, is hired to appraise his late grandmother's house and discovers that every old photograph now contains an extra chair — one that wasn't there before. The house was built by founders who began a ritual to bind a hungry presence into its walls, and the chair is the seat reserved for the next heir. As Orsen investigates, the noises he has rationalized for five years resolve into a voice that knows his name, and the house begins rearranging itself to keep him. To survive, Orsen must complete the founders' interrupted ritual — but doing so means accepting the inheritance of power it offers, a power that corrupts everyone who sits in the chair. In the end, Orsen completes the ritual just enough to trap the presence permanently, then burns the chair and walks away belonging to no house at all.
about_author: Mara Amberdale is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade cataloguing the strange things old houses do when no one is watching. They write horror about inheritance, architecture, and the debts families leave in their foundations.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Orsen arrives at his grandmother's vacant house to conduct the estate appraisal, notebook in hand and five years of rationalized noises behind him. Third-person limited POV. He measures rooms that refuse consistent dimensions. Emotional beat: uneasy professionalism masking dread.

chapters.title: An Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Sorting photographs for the estate lawyer, Orsen notices every family photo now includes an unfamiliar wooden chair — including pictures taken decades ago. His POV. He compares prints with his cousin's digital copies; only hers are unchanged. Emotional beat: the vertigo of realizing memory itself can be edited.

chapters.title: Founders' Deed
chapters.summary: In the county archive, Orsen finds the 1891 deed naming the house's builders, the Aldous siblings, and a codicil describing 'the Seating' — a binding rite left unfinished at their deaths. Archival documents intercut with his POV. Emotional beat: scholarly curiosity curdling into recognition.

chapters.title: The House Appraises Back
chapters.summary: During a second site visit, Orsen's instruments return impossible readings: the house values itself higher every time he enters. His POV. A door he measured at 80 centimeters is now wide enough for the chair to pass through. Emotional beat: the hunter realizing he is the quarry.

chapters.title: Cousin Wren
chapters.summary: Orsen visits Wren, who grew up in the house and refuses to discuss it. Her POV reveals she saw the chair as a child and was told never to sit in it. She begs him to sell the property sight unseen. Emotional beat: the loneliness of being the only one who remembers.

chapters.title: Noises, Explained
chapters.summary: A sleepless night in the house; Orsen catalogs each sound he's explained away over five years and dismantles his own excuses one by one. His POV, diary-form fragments. At 3 a.m., something drags the chair across the upstairs floor toward the landing. Emotional beat: surrender of denial.

chapters.title: The Voice That Knows My Name
chapters.summary: The presence speaks through the heating vents, using recordings of his grandmother's voice spliced into new sentences. First-person POV shift deepens intimacy. It offers him welcome — and calls him 'heir.' Emotional beat: seduction disguised as homecoming.

chapters.title: What the Aldouses Built
chapters.summary: Research chapter: newspaper microfilm reveals the Aldouses' séances, their sudden wealth, and their deaths — each found seated, smiling, emptied. Orsen's POV. The last article mentions a fourth sibling who fled mid-ritual. Emotional beat: pattern recognition as horror.

chapters.title: The Fourth Sibling
chapters.summary: Orsen traces the runaway, Edith Aldous, to a nursing home two counties away. Her POV in a recorded interview: she describes the ritual's three stages — Invitation, Occupation, Coronation — and warns that the house has already finished stage one with him. Emotional beat: inherited guilt and urgency.

chapters.title: Locked In
chapters.summary: Returning to collect his tools, Orsen finds every exit sealed by walls that were not walls yesterday. His POV. The house offers comfort: fire lit, kettle warm, the chair waiting by the window like a dog. Emotional beat: captivity that feels like care.

chapters.title: Wren Breaks the Silence
chapters.summary: Wren, unable to reach Orsen, breaks her lifelong vow and enters the house. Her POV. She finds him half-belonging — speaking in the founders' cadence — and slaps him back to himself. Emotional beat: love as interruption.

chapters.title: Occupation
chapters.summary: Stage two begins: Orsen wakes with dust in his lungs and the house's memories bleeding into his dreams — the Aldouses' rituals, their hunger, their joy. Alternating POV. He starts defending the house to Wren. Emotional beat: corruption experienced as clarity.

chapters.title: The Price of Belonging
chapters.summary: Edith dies peacefully — seated upright, smiling — and the house celebrates with warmth in every room. Orsen's POV. He realizes the presence consumes heirs at coronation and needs him to finish willingly. Emotional beat: grief weaponized against him.

chapters.title: Plans Within Walls
chapters.summary: Wren and Orsen secretly map the house's true geometry using Edith's notes, finding the ritual chamber beneath the cellar stairs. Dual POV. The house eavesdrops through the plumbing. Emotional beat: conspiracy between two people inside a listening body.

chapters.title: The Founders' Mistake
chapters.summary: In Edith's papers, Orsen learns the ritual was meant to bind the presence to the land, not the bloodline — the Aldouses corrupted it to hoard its power. His POV. The unfinished third stage is the flaw: a binding can still be completed correctly. Emotional beat: hope found inside the trap.

chapters.title: Invitation Declined
chapters.summary: The house escalates: it wears grandmother's face in mirrors, replays Orsen's best childhood memories, and finally threatens Wren. His POV. He pretends to accept coronation to buy time. Emotional beat: performance under mortal pressure.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Orsen descends to the ritual chamber carrying salt, iron, and Edith's corrected liturgy while the house screams through every pipe. His POV, near-stream-of-consciousness. The stairs lengthen; the walls applaud. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: Coronation Interrupted
chapters.summary: Climax part one: the presence crowns him prematurely, pouring five years of borrowed belonging into him — power, certainty, the intoxicating sense of finally fitting somewhere. His POV. He nearly says the corrupted words. Emotional beat: temptation at its most beautiful.

chapters.title: The Correct Words
chapters.summary: Climax part two: Wren arrives through a wall the house forgot to grow, reciting Edith's binding with him. Shared POV. The chair shatters mid-coronation; the presence, bound to the land instead of a bloodline, dissipates into the soil like frost burning off. Emotional beat: sacrifice completed together.

chapters.title: Aftermath of a House
chapters.summary: Dawn. The house is only a house — cold, ordinary, slightly shameful in its plainness. Orsen's POV. He files the appraisal honestly, valuing it at almost nothing. Emotional beat: hollow relief, the comedown of survival.

chapters.title: What Orsen Kept
chapters.summary: Epilogue-adjacent: Orsen keeps one photograph — the one with the chair — as proof and warning. His POV. He and Wren split the sale money and agree to meet yearly, an inheritance they chose themselves. Emotional beat: belonging rebuilt on terms of his own.

chapters.title: The New Tenant
chapters.summary: Final chapter, distant third person: months later, the house's new owner mentions to a neighbor that the place 'has good bones' and that sometimes, at night, she hears a chair being set out for someone expected. No resolution offered. Emotional beat: the quiet horror of cycles restarting.
